blocks: The mitigation of motion sickness carries a direct application for symptomatic astronauts, aviators, and sailors.  The causes and physiological variables involved with motion sickness are still under study and the successful expansion of our understanding of the physiology of motion sickness is vital for its prevention.  The data from this experiment suggest that while inspiratory resistance through the ITD is successful in maintaining cerebral bloodflow during motion sickness, it does not prevent the onset of its symptoms. This indicates that cerebral hypoperfusion, though related to the onset of its symptoms, may not be an underlying physiological cause of motion sickness.  However, from our preliminary data we cannot yet conclude the level of efficacy of the ITD in mitigating the symptoms of motion sickness and continued study is warranted.  The development of our protocol and construction of our OVAR chair will permit us to test the role of changes in cardiovascular parameters (blood pressure, heart rate, and cerebral blood flow) in the development and maintenance of motion sickness during OVAR and provide a better understanding of the physiology and possible preventive measures for motion sickness.

Green chemistry and asymmetric catalysis are two very active fields of current research. Green chemistry is a field in which chemists attempt to conduct chemical reactions with the highest efficiency and lowest waste possible.  In a similar vein, researchers in asymmetric catalysis focus on the synthesis of highly valuable chirally pure compounds from achiral starting materials, thus reducing the production of an unwanted—and subsequently discarded—enantiomer.  In this paper, concepts from these two fields were combined in the synthesis of four compounds that may be useful in asymmetric catalysis as reusable chiral solvent media.  These compounds belong to the family of chiral ionic liquids (CILs) and are synthesized from naturally occurring hydroquinine via amine quarternization and anion exchange reactions with good yield.

In recent years, the chemical industry has been increasingly concerned with the “greening” of chemical manufacturing by minimizing energy consumption and waste production.¹  One way to increase efficiency in chemical synthesis is catalysis, where a catalyst is added to a particular reaction to decrease both the reaction time as well as its energy requirement.  Catalysis may also provide selective transformations, producing only the most desirable product, either as a pure chemical compound or as a single isomer from a mixture of possible isomers. This increases efficiency and reduces waste by eliminating purification steps that would otherwise be necessary to remove byproducts.
Supported catalysis as a solution to the separation/recycling problem.

Although catalysis can be a successful strategy in green chemistry, catalysts are often difficult and/or expensive to synthesize, and hence their recycling is essential for the “greening” of a catalytic process.  To this end, many catalysts have been modified and immobilized on solid materials.  This allows the catalysts to be easily recovered, either by filtration or centrifugation, and reused after a simple washing step.²

Recently, new strategies in which catalysts are immobilized in a liquid phase have received a great deal of attention.³  In these strategies, the reactants and products are dissolved in a solvent phase and the catalyst is dissolved in a second support phase that is also a liquid but can be made immiscible with the solvent.  After the reaction, the catalyst can be separated from the product-containing phase for subsequent reuse via a simple phase-separation. The use of a liquid support phase for the catalyst lends a number of advantages over traditional solid supports. The catalyst support phase can be made more miscible with the reactant phase during the reaction by controlling the temperature or agitating the mixture vigorously, thereby increasing the reaction rate via better diffusion. In addition, the polarity and ionic strength of the support phase can be readily tuned to allow for different modes of reactivity that are not commonly available in traditional reaction media (water, gases, organic solvents).

Ionic liquids (ILs) comprise one of the catalyst support systems that possess both of the aforementioned advantages.  An IL is a salt that melts at low temperature (below 100°C), allowing it to exist as a liquid under easily attainable laboratory conditions.  It consists of two parts: a positively charged ion, which usually is derived from an amine-, sulfur-, or phosphorous-containing organic compound, and a negatively-charged ion, which is often a bulky anion such as triflate ([OSO₂CF₃]⁻), tetrafluoroborate (BF₄⁻) or hexafluorophosphate (PF₆⁻) (Figure 1).⁴  ILs readily dissolve polar compounds but are immiscible with non-polar organic solvents due to their ionic character.  As such, they can selectively dissolve a polar catalyst for use with non-polar reaction mixtures, thereby extending the range of reactivity and allowing for catalyst recycling by phase separation.  Another attractive feature of ILs is their low vapor pressure⁵—as salts, ILs produce negligible vapor when compared to traditional organic solvents and can be handled with little loss due to evaporation.
